trial_name: EFFORT Protein — Higher vs Usual Protein Dosing in High-Risk ICU Patients (2023)
citation: Heyland DK, Patel J, Compher C, Rice TW, Bear DE, Lee ZY, et al. The effect of higher protein dosing in critically ill patients with high nutritional risk (EFFORT Protein): an international, multicentre, pragmatic, registry-based randomised trial. Lancet. 2023;401:568-76.
trial_type: RCT — multicentre, pragmatic, registry-based, single-blind, parallel-group
one_liner: In nutritionally high-risk ventilated ICU patients, a strategy of very high protein prescription (≥2.2 g/kg/day, achieved ~1.6 g/kg/day) did not improve time-to-discharge-alive or 60-day mortality compared with usual protein dosing, and showed an exploratory signal of harm in acute kidney injury.

pico.population: Mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients at high nutritional risk (≥1 of: BMI ≥25 or ≥35 kg/m², frailty, sarcopenia, malnutrition, or expected prolonged ventilation), enrolled within 96 h of ICU admission.
pico.intervention: High protein prescription target ≥2.2 g/kg/day (using pre-ICU dry weight; ideal body weight if BMI >30), delivered via any combination of enteral, parenteral, or supplements, encouraged to achieve ≥80% of prescribed protein, continued up to 28 days or ICU discharge/death/oral intake.
pico.comparison: Usual protein prescription target <1.2 g/kg/day, with similar energy and co-interventions.
pico.outcome: Primary: time-to-discharge-alive from hospital up to 60 days. Secondary: 60-day mortality, ICU length of stay, duration of mechanical ventilation, metabolic tolerance (urea).

background.existing_knowledge: Critical illness causes rapid muscle loss and negative nitrogen balance. Protein dosing guidelines varied widely (1.2–2.0 g/kg/day) due to limited and heterogeneous RCT evidence. Mechanistic equipoise existed: higher protein might reduce catabolism but could increase nitrogenous waste and harm in acute kidney injury.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether prescribing higher protein (≥2.2 g/kg/day) versus usual dosing (<1.2 g/kg/day) improves patient-centred outcomes in high-risk ventilated ICU patients was unknown.
background.hypothesis: Higher protein dosing would improve survival and/or accelerate recovery (shorter time-to-discharge-alive from hospital).

methods.design: International, multicentre, pragmatic, registry-based, single-blind (patient), parallel-group RCT. Protocol published before trial completion.

inclusion: Enrolled within 96 h of ICU admission
Expected to remain invasively mechanically ventilated ≥48 h from screening
≥1 high nutritional risk feature: BMI ≥25 kg/m², BMI ≥35 kg/m², Clinical Frailty Scale ≥5, SARC-F ≥4, malnourished by local assessment, or projected duration of mechanical ventilation >4 days
exclusion: Invasively mechanically ventilated >96 h before screening
Expected death or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatments within 7 days
Absence of clinician equipoise regarding protein dose
Requirement for parenteral nutrition only when site lacked products to meet the high-protein target

methods.intervention: Protein prescription target ≥2.2 g/kg/day. Dosing weight: pre-ICU actual 'dry' weight; if BMI >30 kg/m², ideal body weight based on BMI 25 kg/m². Delivery: any combination of enteral nutrition, parenteral nutrition, intravenous amino acids, and/or enteral protein supplements; clinicians encouraged to achieve ≥80% of prescribed protein. Duration: continued up to 28 days post-randomisation, ICU discharge, death, or full oral intake; if readmitted within 28 days, study strategy resumed.
methods.comparison: Protein prescription target <1.2 g/kg/day. Energy targets and other ICU care not protocolised beyond encouragement to avoid overfeeding; route and supportive care at clinician discretion.
methods.blinding: Single-blind (patients not informed of allocation); clinicians unblinded.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 4000 patients to detect a 4% absolute reduction in 60-day mortality (30% to 26%) with 80% power at two-sided 5% significance. Due to COVID-19 feasibility constraints, recruitment was curtailed to ~1200 and the primary outcome was switched to time-to-discharge-alive while allocation remained blinded.
methods.primary_outcome: Time-to-discharge-alive from hospital up to 60 days after ICU admission (competing-risk Fine–Gray model with death as competing event).
secondary_outcomes: Protein and energy delivery (prescribed vs achieved)
methods.follow_up: Primary outcome assessed up to 60 days; nutrition intervention delivered up to 28 days or until ICU discharge/death/full oral intake.

headline_bullets: Higher protein prescription (2.2 vs 1.1 g/kg/day) led to achieved intakes of 1.6 vs 0.9 g/kg/day, with similar energy delivery.
No improvement in time-to-discharge-alive (46.1% vs 50.2%; sHR 0.91, 95% CI 0.77–1.07, P=0.27).
60-day mortality was not reduced (34.6% vs 32.1%; RR 1.08, 95% CI 0.92–1.26).
Higher protein increased urea and showed an exploratory harm signal in acute kidney injury (interaction P=0.001 for discharge-alive; P=0.02 for mortality).

outcomes_table.note: Fine–Gray competing-risk model; death as competing event. Cumulative incidence 46.1% (95% CI 42.0–50.1) vs 50.2% (46.0–54.3). n per group not reported.
Secondary outcome; denominators differ due to withdrawal/loss to follow-up.
Mean ± SD; prescribed 2.2 ± 0.1 vs 1.1 ± 0.2 g/kg/day. Median (IQR) 1.7 (1.3–2.0) vs 1.0 (0.8–1.1).

subgroup_table.subgroup: Acute kidney injury at randomisation (60-day mortality)

safety: Higher protein dosing increased azotaemia: highest urea 14.0 ± 8.5 vs 11.9 ± 7.2 mmol/L (P<0.0001).
Exploratory subgroup analysis suggested possible harm in patients with acute kidney injury (time-to-discharge-alive sHR 0.5, 95% CI 0.4–0.8; 60-day mortality RR 1.4, 95% CI 1.1–1.8).
No other significant differences in adverse events reported.

domains.notes: Central web-based randomisation with permuted blocks (2, 4, 8) and stratification by site; allocation concealed until assignment.
Single-blind (patients); clinicians unblinded. Knowledge of allocation could influence nutrition delivery and discharge decisions, though key outcomes were objective.

Modified ITT: 1329 randomised, 28 excluded post-randomisation (14 per arm) for not receiving intervention, consent withdrawal, or unusable data. Primary analysis included 1297 (4 missing hospital outcomes). 60-day mortality denominators 642 and 648 due to further withdrawals/loss to follow-up.

Protein prescribed: 2.2 ± 0.1 vs 1.1 ± 0.2 g/kg/day; delivered: 1.6 ± 0.5 vs 0.9 ± 0.3 g/kg/day. Protein adequacy (delivered/prescribed): 72.6% vs 75.4%; ≥80% achieved in 45.0% vs 47.1%. Energy delivery similar (14.7 ± 5.5 vs 13.2 ± 4.3 kcal/kg/day). Route of nutrition similar (enteral-only 92.6% vs 91.3%).

Groups broadly comparable: APACHE II 21 (16–27) vs 21 (15–26); SOFA 9 (6–11) vs 9 (6–11); vasopressors 39% vs 41%; baseline AKI 25% vs 23%. Time from ICU admission to randomisation: 38.5 ± 26.4 vs 39.8 ± 27.3 h; time to EN start: 16.0 ± 18.2 vs 16.1 ± 18.1 h.

internal_validity.verdict: Moderate — randomisation and balanced baseline risk support internal validity, but open-label delivery, post-randomisation exclusions, incomplete achievement of the high-dose target, and early outcome switching/curtailed recruitment constrain confidence (particularly for subgroup inferences).

domains.notes: Enrolled mechanically ventilated adults at high nutritional risk across diverse countries and ICU types, increasing generalisability to similar ventilated ICU cohorts. Excluded those without clinician equipoise or expected to die/withdraw life-sustaining treatment within 7 days, limiting applicability to the most imminently dying.

Findings most applicable to ICUs with established dietetic input and access to high-protein enteral feeds, modular protein, and/or parenteral amino acids. Applicability to non-ventilated, lower-risk, or prolonged critical illness beyond 28 days is uncertain.

external_validity.verdict: Generalisability is good for mechanically ventilated, nutritionally high-risk ICU patients in resource-equipped ICUs internationally, but is more limited for low-risk ICU populations, settings without advanced nutrition delivery options, and patients with imminent end-of-life trajectories.

strengths: Large, international, pragmatic, registry-based randomised trial across 85 ICUs.
Enrichment for high nutritional risk patients most likely to be protein-responsive.
Meaningful achieved separation in protein delivery (1.6 ± 0.5 vs 0.9 ± 0.3 g/kg/day) with broadly similar energy delivery.
Appropriate competing-risk methods for the discharge-alive endpoint.
limitations: Recruitment curtailed with a mid-trial primary outcome switch, reducing power for mortality and complicating interpretation.
Open-label delivery with potential performance bias and discharge-practice influence.
Modified intention-to-treat analysis with post-randomisation exclusions and small amounts of missing follow-up data.
High-dose target (≥2.2 g/kg/day) was not achieved on average (mean delivered 1.6 g/kg/day), increasing risk of a 'dose dilution' bias towards null for benefit (and possibly for harm).
No pre-specified functional recovery endpoints (e.g., strength, muscle mass, long-term quality of life), despite mechanistic rationale focused on muscle preservation.

critical_appraisal.summary: EFFORT Protein is a large pragmatic RCT with moderate internal validity due to open-label design, incomplete target achievement, and early termination with outcome switching. External validity is good for high-risk ventilated patients in well-resourced ICUs. The neutral result for the primary outcome and potential harm signal in AKI suggest that routine use of very high early protein is not supported.
strengths: Large sample size and international multicentre design enhance generalisability.
Enrichment for high-risk patients increases clinical relevance.
Meaningful separation in protein delivery despite pragmatic design.
Appropriate statistical methods for competing risks.
weaknesses: Open-label design may introduce performance bias, especially for discharge timing.
Early termination and primary outcome switch reduce power and interpretability for mortality.
High-dose target not achieved, leading to potential dilution of effect.
Post-randomisation exclusions and missing data, though small, could introduce bias.
Lack of functional recovery endpoints limits mechanistic insight.

sections.authors_conclusion: In high nutritional risk ventilated ICU patients, prescribing very high protein (≥2.2 g/kg/day, achieved ~1.6 g/kg/day) did not improve time-to-discharge-alive or 60-day mortality compared with usual dosing. Higher protein increased azotaemia and showed an exploratory harm signal in acute kidney injury, supporting a cautious, individualised approach rather than routine escalation. Achieving sustained high protein delivery was challenging even in trial settings.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Routine use of very high early protein dosing (≥2.2 g/kg/day) in nutritionally high-risk ventilated ICU patients is not supported; a moderate, progressive, and individualised approach is preferred, with caution in acute kidney injury.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Mechanically ventilated adult ICU patients with high nutritional risk, in settings with access to high-protein nutrition products.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Protein is harmful in all patients; the trial does not rule out benefit in specific subgroups or with later, more moderate dosing. The harm signal in AKI is exploratory and requires confirmation.
implementation_caveats: Achieving ≥2.2 g/kg/day is difficult in practice; focus on delivering moderate protein (e.g., 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day) early, with gradual escalation.
Monitor urea and renal function; consider limiting protein in patients with acute kidney injury or rising urea.
Individualise protein dosing based on nutritional risk, organ function, and phase of illness.
Energy delivery should be optimised but not excessive; avoid overfeeding.

controversies.notes: Stopping early (planned n=4000; randomised n=1329) and switching the primary endpoint to time-to-discharge-alive increases susceptibility to outcome switching concerns and limits precision for mortality effects. Time-to-discharge-alive is clinically relevant but partially health-system-dependent (bed capacity, step-down availability, discharge practices).

controversies.topic: Dose dilution and overlap between groups
controversies.notes: The achieved difference (1.6 vs 0.9 g/kg/day) was meaningful but below the prescribed high-dose target (≥2.2 g/kg/day), with overlap at the tails (control maximum 1.9 g/kg/day; intervention minimum 0.1 g/kg/day), which can attenuate true effects.

Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested possible harm in acute kidney injury (time-to-discharge-alive sHR 0.5; 95% CI 0.4–0.8; interaction P=0.001; 60-day mortality RR 1.4; 95% CI 1.1–1.8; interaction P=0.02). A subsequent post hoc analysis further examined kidney injury and suggested differential effects according to renal replacement therapy exposure. Increased urea and urea ≥30 mmol/L provide biological coherence for renal solute burden as a potential mediator or marker of intolerance.

Contemporary commentary emphasised that EFFORT Protein challenges the assumption that 'more protein is always better' early in critical illness and highlighted the need for stage-based and individualised protein strategies (including caution in organ failure phenotypes). Correspondence reinforced uncertainty regarding optimal timing and patient selection.

PRECISe trial reported no functional recovery advantage and signalled worse health-related quality of life and longer time-to-discharge-alive with higher protein provision; it did not reproduce the EFFORT Protein harm signal in acute kidney injury or high SOFA subgroups. An updated meta-analysis reported no overall short-term mortality benefit (RR 0.99; 95% CI 0.90–1.08) and a signal of increased mortality with higher protein among patients with acute kidney injury (RR 1.42; 95% CI 1.11–1.82), alongside higher urea (mean difference 2.31 mmol/L; 95% CI 1.85–2.77). Recent expert recommendations propose lower protein (0.2–0.9 g/kg/day) during the first ICU week rather than 'standard' 1.0–1.3 g/kg/day, with escalation back to 1.0–1.3 g/kg/day by the end of week 1.

context_related_trials.relation: A protocolised, blinded RCT in mechanically ventilated ICU patients that reported no functional recovery advantage and signalled worse health-related quality of life and longer time-to-discharge-alive with higher protein provision; did not reproduce the EFFORT Protein harm signal in acute kidney injury or high SOFA subgroups.

unresolved_questions: Optimal protein dose and timing in different phases of critical illness and in subgroups (e.g., AKI, frailty, obesity).
Whether functional recovery or long-term quality of life is affected by protein dosing.
The role of protein dosing in patients without high nutritional risk.
How to individualise protein prescription based on dynamic metabolic tolerance (e.g., urea kinetics).

numbers_to_remember: Primary outcome: time-to-discharge-alive 46.1% vs 50.2% (sHR 0.91, 95% CI 0.77–1.07, P=0.27)
AKI subgroup: mortality RR 1.4 (95% CI 1.1–1.8, interaction P=0.02)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In high-risk ventilated ICU patients, very high early protein did not improve outcomes and may harm those with acute kidney injury; use moderate, progressive, individualised dosing.
